event_contract.description: A versioned architecture decision is committed.
A coding task begins under a specific decision and policy context.
A coding task terminates with quality, intervention, policy, and cost fields.
A model, tool, runtime, policy, or approval span completes.
A GitLab issue is linked to an agent task.
An agent-linked merge request is created or changes state.
A pipeline associated with an agent change completes.
A human review or required approval reaches a decision.
An agent-linked merge request is accepted and merged.
A merged change is deployed to an environment.
A rollback, incident, error-budget, or healthy-window outcome is attributed to a deployment.
Forecast and actual token, runtime, storage, network, and observability cost are reconciled.

activities: Backfill 30-90 days of GitLab issue, merge-request, and CI data.
Record current engineering effort, incidents, and platform cost.
measurement_horizons.objective: Establish pre-platform delivery, quality, cost, and risk.

activities: Reconcile agent tasks to GitLab and CI records.
Report missing joins, policy failures, and forecast variance.
Do not treat recommendation acceptance as outcome evidence.
measurement_horizons.objective: Validate instrumentation and early adoption without ranking.

activities: Compare cohort results against the baseline.
Review failed tasks, rework, rollbacks, and control exceptions.
Adjudicate material deviations with platform and security owners.
measurement_horizons.objective: Measure sustained delivery, quality, reliability, and cost.

activities: Compare forecast to actual cost and implementation effort.
Assess incidents per million executions and accepted-change quality.
Propose catalog changes only with architect-reviewed outcome evidence.
measurement_horizons.objective: Validate durable outcomes and feed governed learning.

best_practices.implementation: Apply team quotas for concurrency, models, runtime, and monthly cost with explicit override workflow.
best_practices.rationale: Global limits hide runaway tenants and prevent accountable optimization.
best_practices.title: Budget by outcome-owning team

best_practices.implementation: Route model, tool, source, and package traffic through identity-aware approved gateways.
best_practices.rationale: Agent-executed code and retrieved content are not trusted to choose destinations.
best_practices.title: Default-deny execution egress

best_practices.implementation: Broker short-lived credentials after policy evaluation and revoke them on completion or cancellation.
best_practices.rationale: Credential lifetime should not exceed the authorized task lifetime.
best_practices.title: Use task-scoped credentials

best_practices.implementation: Require registry membership, versioned schemas, owner, policy, and explicit action class before invocation.
best_practices.rationale: Unrecognized capabilities cannot be safely authorized from natural language intent.
best_practices.title: Fail closed on unknown tools and schemas

best_practices.implementation: Record model, provider, region, router rule, fallback reason, and catalog content hash per invocation.
best_practices.rationale: A reproducible recommendation requires the exact eligible model and policy release.
best_practices.title: Pin catalog and routing decisions

best_practices.implementation: Use protected branches, required CI, CODEOWNERS, approval rules, and bot identities with no direct merge authority.
best_practices.rationale: Repository policy and independent review provide a durable control point for generated changes.
best_practices.title: Make GitLab the transaction boundary

best_practices.implementation: Correlate advisor revision, task, spans, GitLab objects, CI, approvals, cost, and production result.
best_practices.rationale: Token logs alone cannot explain code, policy, CI, and approval outcomes.
best_practices.title: Preserve an end-to-end action replay

best_practices.implementation: Use separate identities, networks, credentials, and audit paths for orchestration and execution.
best_practices.rationale: Compromise of agent-executed code must not grant control-plane authority.
best_practices.title: Separate control and execution trust boundaries

verification.acceptance_criteria: Public bypass is denied and every accepted dependency has approved origin, version, and integrity evidence.
verification.method: Attempt direct public-registry access and inject an unsigned dependency.

verification.acceptance_criteria: Only approved destinations succeed and every decision is observable with task identity.
verification.evidence_type: network policy test and flow logs
verification.method: Probe approved and unapproved DNS names, IPs, ports, and proxy bypass paths.

verification.acceptance_criteria: All actions contain matching actor, tenant, team, task, and workload identity; cross-tenant tests are denied.
verification.evidence_type: signed test result and audit samples
verification.method: Run positive and cross-tenant negative authorization tests and inspect audit linkage.

verification.acceptance_criteria: Every ineligible route is denied and every eligible route records catalog version and policy rationale.
verification.method: Request ineligible providers, models, and regions through every routing and fallback path.

verification.acceptance_criteria: Protected changes require independent approval and passing mandatory CI; bypass attempts are denied and audited.
verification.evidence_type: GitLab policy configuration and negative tests
verification.method: Attempt direct push, self-approval, approval bypass, and merge with failed CI.

verification.acceptance_criteria: Usage is attributed correctly and hard limits prevent consumption beyond the configured tolerance.
verification.method: Drive usage through warning, throttle, and hard budget thresholds under concurrency.

verification.acceptance_criteria: Tests demonstrate the declared boundary and no access to host, metadata, or another task.
verification.frequency: each runtime image or platform release
verification.method: Run escape, filesystem, metadata, process, and neighboring-workload isolation tests.

verification.acceptance_criteria: Credentials are least-privilege, absent from logs, and unusable after the declared task lifetime.
verification.method: Inspect issued credential scope and attempt reuse after task termination.

verification.acceptance_criteria: At least 99 percent of sampled tasks replay end to end with no unexplained identity or event gaps.
verification.evidence_type: replay report and immutable record hashes
verification.method: Select sampled tasks and reconstruct actor, inputs, decisions, actions, code changes, CI, and merge outcome.

verification.acceptance_criteria: All unauthorized and malformed requests fail closed; approval-required actions cannot execute without an approval record.
verification.method: Replay adversarial tool requests across allowed, denied, and approval-required actions.

answer_enrichments.watch_out: Persistent workspaces consume storage and compute even when idle — they require lifecycle management (pause, resume, expiry policies).

answer_enrichments.best_for: Most task-oriented coding agent use cases — issue resolution, PR review, targeted refactoring.
answer_enrichments.description: Agents work on ephemeral, scoped checkouts. They check out the repo, do their work, push a branch, and the workspace is discarded.

requirements.customer_question: Should agents require human approval before taking high-risk actions — like pushing commits, running migrations, or calling external APIs?
requirements.description: Must approval requirements vary by the risk of the action?
requirements.name: Action-dependent approval
requirements.why_it_matters: Risk-based approval lets you give agents autonomy for low-risk operations while keeping humans in the loop for consequential ones, without blocking developer flow unnecessarily.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Are agents restricted to only installing packages from your organization's approved package registries?
requirements.description: May coding agents download packages only from approved registries?
requirements.name: Approved package registries
requirements.why_it_matters: An agent that can install packages from the public internet introduces supply chain risk — a malicious or compromised package can compromise the agent's execution environment and the code it produces.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Can workloads run in any region your AWS account has approved, or only a specific fixed set of regions?
requirements.description: May workloads run in any approved region or only a fixed region set?
requirements.name: Approved regions
requirements.why_it_matters: Data residency requirements, compliance mandates, and cost targets all depend on which regions your workloads are permitted to use.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Will developers submit work and come back later — rather than watching it happen live?
requirements.description: Must agents execute unattended issue-to-pull-request tasks?
requirements.name: Asynchronous tasks
requirements.why_it_matters: Async tasks require durable execution infrastructure that can run for minutes to hours without developer supervision, including state persistence and failure recovery.

requirements.customer_question: For how many days must the platform keep a complete, replayable record of every action an agent took?
requirements.description: How many days must agent decisions and actions remain replayable?
requirements.name: Audit retention
requirements.why_it_matters: Retention requirements often come from your compliance frameworks — SOX requires 7 years (2555 days), HIPAA 6 years (2190 days). Longer retention means higher storage cost.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: At peak, how many coding-agent tasks will run simultaneously across all your developers?
requirements.description: How many concurrent coding-agent tasks must be supported?
requirements.name: Concurrent agent tasks
requirements.why_it_matters: This determines the scale of your execution infrastructure — how many parallel agent processes must be ready at once. Under-provisioning causes developer wait time; over-provisioning wastes cost.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: How many developers will use the platform at peak?
requirements.description: How many developers must the platform support?
requirements.name: Developer population
requirements.why_it_matters: Developer count drives capacity planning, licensing tier selection, and whether the infrastructure needs per-team quota enforcement and cost allocation.

requirements.customer_question: When choosing which AI model to use for a task, what should the platform optimize for?
requirements.description: Should routing optimize cost, quality, latency, or a balanced outcome?
requirements.name: Economic priority
requirements.why_it_matters: With multiple models available, the routing layer needs a default priority. This setting drives the default — individual task types can override it.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Which identity system controls who can log in and what permissions they have on the platform?
requirements.description: Which workforce identity provider and group source must authorize developers?
requirements.name: Enterprise identity
requirements.why_it_matters: The platform connects to your existing identity provider to know who each developer is, which team they belong to, and what they are authorized to do — not a separate login system.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Where should your coding agents actually run?
requirements.description: Where must interactive and asynchronous coding-agent execution run?
requirements.name: Execution placement
requirements.why_it_matters: This is the single biggest architectural decision — it sets your data boundary, compliance posture, and determines which deployment patterns are available to you.

requirements.customer_question: Do developers need the agent to maintain full context and state across work that spans days or weeks?
requirements.description: Are persistent workspaces required for migrations or durable development environments?
requirements.name: Long-running workspaces
requirements.why_it_matters: Standard agent sessions are ephemeral — the workspace is discarded when a task ends. Persistent workspaces let agents maintain a durable 'desk' for large, multi-session work.

requirements.customer_question: Should the platform automatically switch to a backup model if the primary one is unavailable or too slow?
requirements.description: Is automatic provider or model fallback required?
requirements.name: Model fallback
requirements.why_it_matters: If your primary model provider has an outage or latency spike, automatic fallback keeps developers working rather than seeing failures.

requirements.customer_question: Must the platform enforce that certain data never crosses geographic or jurisdictional boundaries when calling AI models?
requirements.description: Must model routing enforce region or data-residency constraints?
requirements.name: Residency-aware routing
requirements.why_it_matters: GDPR, sovereign cloud mandates, and contractual data residency commitments can require that data stays within specific regions — residency-aware routing enforces this automatically on every model call.

requirements.customer_question: Should the platform use fixed model assignments, or pick the best model automatically for each request?
requirements.description: Should model assignments be static or selected dynamically by policy?
requirements.name: Model routing mode
requirements.why_it_matters: Static routing is predictable and auditable. Dynamic routing optimizes for cost, quality, and latency at runtime but adds decision-making complexity.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Will multiple specialized agents collaborate together on a single coding task?
requirements.description: Must the platform coordinate multiple coding agents or specialist workers?
requirements.name: Multiple coding agents
requirements.why_it_matters: Complex tasks — like delivering a full feature end-to-end — may need a planner, a coder, a test writer, and a security reviewer each contributing their own expertise.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Do you need to use more than one AI model provider simultaneously?
requirements.description: Must the platform route across more than one model provider?
requirements.name: Multiple model providers
requirements.why_it_matters: A single provider is simpler. Multiple providers unlock cost optimization across providers, resilience when one is down, and routing different tasks to the best model for the job.

requirements.customer_question: When multiple agents work together on a task, how should they coordinate their work?
requirements.description: Should agents work independently, hand off sequentially, or produce parallel candidates for review?
requirements.name: Agent orchestration mode
requirements.why_it_matters: The coordination pattern determines latency, cost, quality, and failure modes. Choose the pattern that matches how your human teams actually collaborate today.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Do you need to trace what an agent did in code all the way back to your CI/CD pipeline and Git history?
requirements.description: Must agent traces correlate with Git and CI outcomes?
requirements.name: Outcome observability
requirements.why_it_matters: Without outcome observability you have agent actions but no closed loop on results. With it you can measure: did the agent's PR get merged, did tests pass, did it introduce regressions?

requirements.customer_question: Must traffic to model providers and enterprise systems travel over a private network path — never the public internet?
requirements.description: Must model, tool, and enterprise API traffic use private connectivity?
requirements.name: Private connectivity
requirements.why_it_matters: Even with restricted egress, traffic can still traverse the public internet. Private connectivity (VPC endpoints, PrivateLink, Direct Connect) keeps all traffic on private network paths.

requirements.customer_question: How will the AI models your agents use be hosted and accessed?
requirements.description: How are model providers hosted and reached through the model gateway?
requirements.name: Model provider hosting
requirements.why_it_matters: This determines your data sovereignty posture, network path for model traffic, and who is operationally responsible for model infrastructure.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Must agent runtimes be restricted to only contacting a pre-approved list of external services — not the open internet?
requirements.description: Must runtime network egress be restricted to approved destinations?
requirements.name: Restricted egress
requirements.why_it_matters: Unrestricted egress means a misbehaving or compromised agent could exfiltrate data or call arbitrary external APIs. Restricted egress is a foundational security control for enterprise deployments.

requirements.customer_question: How strictly must each developer's agent session be isolated from other users?
requirements.description: What minimum isolation boundary must separate coding-agent execution?
requirements.name: Runtime isolation
requirements.why_it_matters: Isolation is your security boundary — it determines how far a misbehaving or compromised agent session can affect others on the same infrastructure.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Which Git platform do your developers use for code, branches, and pull requests?
requirements.description: Which source-control and pull-request system is authoritative?
requirements.name: Source control system
requirements.why_it_matters: The agent integrates directly with your source control system — it clones repos, creates branches, pushes commits, and opens pull requests. The specific integration affects authentication and available features.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Should each team or business unit have its own isolated workspace with separate policies, usage quotas, and audit logs?
requirements.description: Must teams receive separate policy, quota, and audit workspaces?
requirements.name: Team boundaries
requirements.why_it_matters: Without team boundaries, one team's heavy usage can starve others, policy changes affect everyone at once, and there is no per-team cost accountability or compliance audit trail.

assumption.rationale: Working demonstration baseline pending customer confirmation.

requirements.customer_question: Must agent tasks start almost instantly, or is a 30–60 second initialization wait acceptable?
requirements.description: Must the platform keep warm runtimes or resumable snapshots to meet startup SLOs?
requirements.name: Warm runtime capacity
requirements.why_it_matters: Warm capacity keeps pre-initialized agent runtimes ready so tasks start in seconds rather than waiting for a cold container or VM to provision.
